Yes, a Friday afternoon deploy is outside the normal window, but it isn't banned. Production deploys run Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [1][2].

Other things to plan for:

- **Longer canary:** Since October 12, a deploy sits in the canary cell for 45 minutes before it can be promoted, up from 20 minutes [2].
- **Data-plane waves:** Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` roll out in waves with 30 minutes between them, so they take about two and a half hours to reach every cell [2].
- **Ledger billing freeze:** Normal changes to Ledger are blocked from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually on the 2nd [3]. Since the last business day of October was Friday, October 30, that freeze is in effect now.
- **Rollbacks:** These are allowed at any time without approval [1][2].
- **Emergency fixes:** During an incident, the incident commander can approve skipping the bake with `/deploy expedite`, and the expedite is logged in `#eng-changes` [2].

A critical lab result must reach the ordering clinician within **60 minutes**. If that clinician can't be reached within **30 minutes**, the result goes to the on-call medical director [1].

**If you can't reach the ordering clinician:**
- Call the Halcyon answering service at **555-0144** and choose **option 2**. This pages the on-call medical director [2].
- If there's no callback within 10 minutes, the answering service pages the backup [2].
- Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers. Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [2].
- Record the notification in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network and is the person who receives critical results when the ordering clinician can't be reached [2]. The November rota is the one in the knowledge base. Today is October 31, so check that the rota covering your shift is in effect.

Emergency access to a customer workspace lasts **2 hours**. A second engineer must approve it [1]. That is shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [1].

**Approval**
- A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation approves the request in Teleport [1].
- You cannot approve your own request, and the approver must not be on the same case [1].
- Every request must reference an open support case or a declared incident ID. "Curiosity" and "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [1].

**Scope**
- Access is read-only by default [1].
- Write access, such as editing a pipeline on the customer's behalf, needs the customer's written consent recorded in the case first [1].

**If you need more time**
- Request access again with an update on the case [1].

To start, run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>` [1].

No. Removing the name doesn't make it acceptable. Public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants are not approved for Halcyon staff on any device, including personal phones [1]. The approved-tools policy also says "de-identified" is not a loophole, because removing a name is not enough to make a case non-identifiable. Treat any patient details as PHI [1].

Approved options:
- **Quillon Ambient** can handle PHI, but only as an AI scribe that drafts visit notes, and only at the pilot clinics (Riverside and Elm Park). Patient verbal consent is required, and a clinician must review and sign every note [1].
- **Meridian draft replies** can handle PHI for drafting patient portal responses inside Meridian EHR. A clinician must edit or approve each one before it is sent [1].
- **Halcyon Assist** is for policy questions only. Don't paste patient details into it, even without names [1].

If you need a patient's history summarized, use Meridian EHR, which is the approved system holding the full clinical record [5].

If you already pasted patient information into a public chatbot, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [3].

rows.answer:
**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's chart at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1].

The root cause analysis identified three contributing causes [1]:

- **Weak fallback matching.** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, without notice. The interface engine, Switchyard, could no longer find the MRN and fell back to matching on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume.
- **No monitoring of fallback matches.** Nobody was alerted that all Bayline results were using the fallback rule.
- **No change-notice obligation.** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes.

A medical assistant at Riverside spotted a potassium result that didn't match the patient's history on July 23. The charge nurse reported it and stopped the Bayline feed. The MRN mapping was corrected and the feed restored on July 24 [1]. Two patients had abnormal results go to another chart, and their follow-up was delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].

Halcyon's documents don't use the term "incident commander." The closest equivalent is the **charge nurse**, who coordinates the immediate response to a patient safety event. If there is no charge nurse on shift, the **clinic manager** takes that role.

- **Large clinics:** the designated charge nurse coordinates the immediate response to any patient safety event [1].
- **Medium and small clinics:** a charge nurse is designated whenever two or more RNs are on shift. Otherwise the clinic manager fills the role [1].
- **What the role covers:** the charge nurse assigns who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records involved [7].
- **Sentinel events:** the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [7]. The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network [2].

Before the charge nurse steps in, staff must first make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, which calls for 911 in urgent cases [7][4].

Halcyon doesn't use a "DPA" for this. It requires a **signed business associate agreement (BAA)** and a **security risk assessment**, both in place before any patient data moves.

**What Halcyon needs before a vendor gets PHI**

- **Signed BAA.** Any vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate. Halcyon must have a signed BAA before any PHI is disclosed, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [6].
- **Security risk assessment.** Any tool or vendor that will handle PHI needs one [7]. New systems that hold PHI need it before go-live [8][10].
- **Systems inventory entry.** The system must be added to the clinical and business systems inventory before go-live [7][8].
- **Clinical safety review, for clinical use.** The CMIO must complete a clinical safety review [7]. For example, expanding the AI scribe beyond its pilot clinics needs a CSCAB decision and a clinical safety review [5].
- **Contact.** For AI tools, email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) [7].

**Current vendor status**

- Quillon Ambient has its BAA executed (July 30, 2026) and a completed security risk assessment (July 2026) [5].
- Tallgrass Survey Co. has no executed BAA. Its security risk assessment passed with conditions in September 2026, and no PHI may be shared until the BAA is signed [6].
- The register for Polyglen Interpreting shows a BAA dated 2025-03-03 but no security risk assessment date [4].
- The Brightwater Billing row has a security risk assessment date (2026-06-01) but the BAA field is blank, so I can't confirm its BAA status from the register [1].

Note that the Northwind Labs vendor register uses DPAs and security reviews, which is the framing in your question. That register is a separate organization's records, so it doesn't set Halcyon's requirements [Northwind vendor register].

Northwind has no EHR, so it has no direct equivalent of break-the-glass for clinical records. Its closest counterpart is emergency access to customer workspaces, which covers a different kind of data and works in a different way [2].

**Halcyon's break-the-glass (Meridian EHR)**
- Lets a workforce member open a chart outside their normal patient relationships when care needs it [1].
- The user picks a reason (Emergency care, Coverage, or Other) and types a justification. No one approves it in the moment [1].
- Access lasts until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [1].
- Every event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. Unclear reasons go to the manager [1].
- Misuse is a privacy incident and can lead to sanctions up to termination [1].
- The compliance team also reviews EHR access logs monthly with anomaly detection [3].

**Northwind's emergency access to customer workspaces**
- Used only when there is an open support case or declared incident. Every request must cite the case or incident ID [2].
- The engineer requests access through a CLI command, and a second engineer must approve it in Teleport before access is granted. The approver cannot be the requester or be on the same case [2].
- Access is read-only by default. Write access also needs the customer's written consent [2].
- It expires after 2 hours, much shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [2][4].
- Sessions are recorded and kept for one year. The customer's audit log shows the access, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security reviews a sample of sessions weekly, and every session that used write access [2].

**Main differences**
- **Approval:** Halcyon grants access immediately and reviews afterward. Northwind requires a second engineer's approval before access starts.
- **Default scope:** Halcyon's access covers the full chart for the shift. Northwind's is read-only unless the customer consents to write access.
- **Duration:** 12 hours for Halcyon, 2 hours for Northwind.
- **Customer visibility:** Northwind tells the customer's admins. The Halcyon source does not mention notifying patients.
- **Review:** Halcyon's Privacy Officer reviews each event within 2 business days. Northwind's security team samples sessions weekly.

**Short answer: No, not for the sensitive data these policies cover.** At Halcyon, Slack is never allowed for patient data. At Northwind, the most sensitive class is barred from Slack, and the rest is only shared on a need-to-know basis.

**Halcyon Health**
- PHI may never go into Slack, and the rule has no exception for DMs. PHI may only live in the EHR, the practice management system, and approved systems on the intranet [3][1].
- The systems inventory lists Slack as "Never, including DMs" [1].
- If PHI is exposed, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [3].

**Northwind Labs**
- Restricted data, such as customer event payloads, credentials, and encryption keys, never leaves production and is never allowed in tickets or Slack [2].
- Don't paste event payloads into Slack or support replies. Use field names and counts instead [4].
- Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared on a need-to-know basis. The policy doesn't explicitly ban Slack for it, but it doesn't approve it either [2].
- Report suspected incidents in `#security-help` [2].

I didn't find any approved exception to these rules at either organization.

You need sign-off from the **Platform team's change approver, Oluwaseun Adeyemi**, or his delegate, Kofi Mensah [7].

Here's the chain:

- **The rule:** Archived event payloads sit in Driftwood, and their 365-day default retention is enforced by object-storage lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets. Changing those rules is a normal change under the production change approval policy [2].
- **The owner:** Driftwood is owned by PLAT (Platform) [5].
- **The approver:** The PLAT change approver is Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate [7].

The process, from the production change approval policy [4]:

1. Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections of the template.
2. Request review from the approver (or delegate) as a CODEOWNERS reviewer.
3. Because this changes how long customer data is kept, also link an ADR from the PR, per the engineering handbook.
4. Approvals are valid for 7 days, so re-request if the change hasn't shipped by then.

Two other points from the same policy [4]:

- If you're shortening retention for Enterprise customers whose contracts reference a retention period, the account team must give 30 days' customer notice.
- The holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, and only standard and emergency changes are allowed then.

Note that the v2 retention standard (effective September 15, 2026) supersedes v1, which listed 400 days [1][2].

rows.answer:
The helpdesk tool is Hollowpine Software Co.'s customer support ticketing (register ID VEN-031). It is running under security exception SEC-EX-117, which the Head of Security approved on August 24, 2026 [2]. The DPA is still not signed. The draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines with legal have been open since August. The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [2].

**How long the sign-off lasts:** The information security policy says exceptions require written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [5]. Counting 90 days from August 24 gives about November 22, 2026. That is my calculation, not a date stated in the register, so confirm the exact expiry on SEC-EX-117. The register says that if the DPA is still unsigned when the exception lapses, Support Operations must either renew the exception or move ticket intake back to email [2].

**Other conditions:**
- The security review is a conditional pass. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [2].
- Support must not paste restricted data into tickets, and must not attach event payloads, credentials or encryption keys [2].

rows.answer:
Changing the reminder send time is a **significant change**, so it needs three approvals:

1. **System steward: Felix Brandt.** The reminder scheduler, Pillbox, is owned by Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), and Felix Brandt is that team's steward [1][5].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: Dr. Anjali Rao, CMIO**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [1].
3. **Review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1]. The change goes in as a change request with a CHG number, brought by the project lead [2].

Patient-facing reminders count as significant changes under the policy [1]. Because of IR-0412, where two reminder runners ran at once, any scheduler cutover also needs a written runbook that says how double-sending is prevented [1][4].

The only exception is an emergency change to stop ongoing patient harm. The on-call medical director can approve that, and CSCAB reviews it at its next meeting [1]. A routine schedule change doesn't qualify.

The fix would need three approvals, and Integration Services' steward is the first one.

1. **System steward, Integration Services: Owen Mbeki.** The Bayline HL7 feed into Switchyard is owned by Integration Services (INT) [5]. Each owning team's steward approves changes to that team's systems [2].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: CMIO Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei.** Changes to results routing are significant changes and need this sign-off [2]. The fix to the matching and MRN handling affects how results are routed, so it falls in this category.
3. **CSCAB review.** The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board reviews significant changes at its weekly meeting, Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]. The project lead brings the release to CSCAB as a change request [6].

If the fix had to go in as an emergency to stop ongoing patient harm, the on-call medical director could approve it, and CSCAB would review it at its next meeting [2]. The on-call medical director for November is listed in the rota [4].

Any cutover of the feed or Switchyard job must also have a written runbook that states how double-running is prevented [2]. The Wren project already plans integrated retesting of Switchyard's reference lab interfaces with Integration Services [6].

I based the Switchyard-to-INT link on the vendor matrix. I did not check the systems inventory, which would confirm the owning team.

Yes, as far as the knowledge base shows. INC-2291 had four action items, and each is marked done or shipped.

1. **Validate certificate chains in the rotation job before publishing (platform team, due Aug 28):** marked done [2].
2. **Lower the canary handshake-failure alert to page on sustained failures over 5 minutes (ingest team):** marked done [2].
3. **Reduce gateway TLS session ticket lifetime from 4 hours to 30 minutes (ingest team, due Sep 15):** the September 2026 changelog says it shipped ahead of the due date [4].
4. **Add a "TLS handshake errors" panel to the ingest dashboard (observability):** marked done [2].

The product spec sets the Enterprise limit at **500 million rows per workspace**, up from 50 million on Growth [3]. This is a planning target, not a confirmed shipped limit. The spec is a draft goal for the Enrich step, and the feature is still in private beta, with GA targeted for January 2027 [4].

Two related points:
- **Snapshot rebuild time:** A runner rebuilds its reference-table snapshot from scratch after a restart or when CDC lag exceeds 10 minutes. For a 50M-row table, that takes about 25 minutes [2]. The proposed RFC-031 snapshot persistence targets under 90 seconds of restore time for a 50M-row table, but its approval was still pending when the RFC was written [2].
- **Forced refreshes:** Enterprise workspaces can call the reference-table refresh endpoint once every 2 minutes [1]. Customers rarely need it, because change data capture keeps snapshots current [1].

I didn't find a document that confirms the 500M figure is in effect today, or any per-cell capacity limits that would apply to it. If you need a commitment for a customer, check with the Tributary product owner before quoting it.

rows.answer:
When a customer goes over their limit, the API returns **HTTP 429**. The response includes a `Retry-After` header that gives the number of seconds to wait before retrying [1].

**How the customer knows when to retry:** The `Retry-After` header tells them how long to wait. Northwind's SDKs honour that header automatically and back off exponentially, so customers using the SDKs usually don't need to write retry logic themselves [1]. Customers calling the HTTP API directly should read `Retry-After` and wait that long before resending.

**Other details that matter:**
- Limits apply per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- If an endpoint isn't included in the customer's plan, the API returns HTTP 403 rather than 429 [1].

**Limits by plan:** For the main ingest endpoint, `POST /v2/events`, the limits are 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 req/s on Growth and 10,000 req/s on Enterprise by default [1]. The full table covers other endpoints, such as pipeline runs and the audit log export [1].

I didn't find documentation of the exact body text of the 429 response, so check the public API docs if customers need that detail. The rate limits page says the public docs copy it on each release [1].

rows.answer:
You need sign-off from **Oluwaseun Adeyemi**, the PLAT change approver. Their delegate is **Kofi Mensah** [1].

- **Why PLAT:** Hydrant is owned by PLAT, and its per-cell floor and ceiling live in the PLAT infrastructure repo. Changing them is a normal change, which needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [3][5].
- **No security sign-off:** Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't a Restricted service, so Security isn't required [3].
- **Current values:** us-east runs with a floor of 16 and a ceiling of 64 gateway replicas [2].
- **How to request it:** Add the `change:normal` label to the PR, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver (or delegate) as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Approvals are valid for 7 days, so re-request if it hasn't shipped by then [5].

Before you raise the ceiling, consider the alert. If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because hitting the ceiling usually signals a gateway problem rather than real traffic [3]. Raising the ceiling may be right, but it's worth checking with Data Plane whether the us-east pinning reflects real load or a gateway issue. Questions about Hydrant go to #team-platform [3].

- **runner**: executes customer pipelines. Stores partition state in local RocksDB and reference-table snapshots. Owner: DP [1].

Your deploy will bake in the canary cell for **45 minutes** before it can be promoted automatically [1]. The October 2026 pipeline change raised this from the 20 minutes in the engineering handbook [1][2]. The note says it overrides the handbook where they differ, and the handbook will be updated to match [1].

Promotion also needs two checks that are new in October:
- Zero sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary.
- Runner consumer lag growing by no more than 2 minutes during the bake [1].

The existing error-rate and p95-latency checks, which must stay within 10% of baseline, are unchanged [1].

If your change is under `ingest/` or `runner/`, it then rolls out in waves with 30 minutes between each: `us-central`, `us-west`, `us-east`, then `eu-central` [1]. Other services go to all cells at once after canary [1].

**No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand.** The runbook step is out of date. Hydrant, the gateway autoscaler, has replaced it in us-west, and it will revert a manual change within 2 minutes [2]. The runbook still lists the manual command [1], so it needs updating.

What to do instead:

- **Check Hydrant first.** It scales up when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, adding 25% of current replicas (at least 2) per step [2]. With CPU above 80%, it should already be scaling. us-west's replica range is 10 (floor) to 48 (ceiling) [3].
- **Check the ceiling.** If us-west sits at 48 for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call. A ceiling hit usually means a gateway problem, not real traffic [2].
- **Check TLS handshake errors.** The runbook's other steps still apply: confirm which cell is affected and look at gateway TLS handshake errors first, since INC-2291 was a TLS failure [1][5].
- **Pin the count only if you must.** For example, while debugging a bad gateway build, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds last at most 4 hours and need no approval. Release early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [2].

If the 5xx rate keeps climbing and Hydrant isn't adding replicas, escalate to the Data Plane primary. The runbook's SEV-1 and SEV-2 rules also apply: declare with `/incident declare` if the outage is full or partial [1][4].

I can't see live metrics, so I haven't confirmed the current replica count or Hydrant's status.

By default, archived events stay in the attic (Driftwood) for **365 days** before deletion. This is the current default under version 2.0 of the customer data retention standard, effective September 15, 2026 [2]. Version 1.0 set it at 400 days, but v2 supersedes it [2].

- Deletion is enforced by object-storage lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets, which delete objects once they pass the retention period for their workspace [2].
- Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags, so a workspace's retention can differ from the default [2].
- Enterprise customers can contract for longer archive retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2].

"The attic" is an informal name for Driftwood, the long-term event archive. Older documents call it the cold store [3].

The page does say limits are per workspace and that the Growth plan's rates apply to the listed endpoints. Growth examples include 2,000 req/s on `POST /v2/events` and 10 req/s on `POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs` [1]. Those figures don't apply to `/v2/destinations`.

The table is owned by Data Plane for ingest endpoints and Workspace Experience for the management API [1]. Ask one of those teams whether `/v2/destinations` is covered, or whether it has a separate limit.

- **If you're working toward the January 31, 2027 deadline:** you have until then to finish, and access would be suspended only if you're still incomplete after February 14, 2027 [1].

**No, don't discard the vaccines yet.** A reading of 10 °C is outside the 2–8 °C range, but the stock may still be usable. The clinical pharmacist decides that [1].

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use." Keep it refrigerated in a working unit, and record the reading, the time and how long the fridge has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** They check with the manufacturers whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** It is a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine was given. It is a higher level if a patient received affected vaccine [1].
4. **Give no vaccine from the affected stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

- **Emergency system changes** to stop ongoing patient harm [1][4].

Wren is the codename for the Meridian EHR upgrade to release 2027.1, so the vendor is Meridian Clinical Systems [3]. Its P1 first response is 15 minutes, and it is staffed 24/7 [2].

Steps during the cutover:

- **Open a ticket with the IT Service Desk first** (extension 4357, or the intranet Service Desk tile). The Service Desk contacts the vendor, tracks the response, and pages the owning team's system steward for any P1 [2]. Clinic staff should not call the vendor directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [2].
- **Expect a live bridge line.** For any scheduled Meridian EHR upgrade, Meridian staffs a bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window, in addition to 24/7 support [2].
- **A P1 is** a system down or unusable at one or more clinics, or any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, such as results not arriving [2].

The 15-minute figure is a contractual first response from a qualified engineer, not a resolution time [2]. If Meridian misses it, the Service Desk escalates to Meridian's account manager and tells the steward [2].

The cutover is planned for Saturday, February 6, 2027, from 22:00 Eastern, with 6 hours of downtime [1]. Note that the matrix lists Meridian's P1 terms, but I did not find a specific Wren cutover escalation contact beyond the Service Desk and the bridge line.

Four items are not stocked at any clinic, so each must be ordered for the named patient: **Td, PCV21, Meningococcal B, and HPV 9-valent**. These are the Tier 3 items [1].

- **Td** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe), self-pay $46. Tdap is preferred; Td is only given on request [1].
- **Pneumococcal conjugate PCV21** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe), self-pay $280. Only when the clinician specifies PCV21 [1].
- **Meningococcal B vaccine** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe), self-pay $190 per dose. For ages 16–23 or on specialist advice [1].
- **HPV vaccine, 9-valent** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe), self-pay $295 per dose. For ages 9–45 [1].

For Tier 3, the clinical pharmacist places the order with the wholesaler, and allow 5 business days [1]. Tier 2 items (such as RZV, hepatitis B and ceftriaxone) are stocked only at hub clinics and transfer to other sites within 2 business days, so they are not "not stocked at all" [1][2].

Under the current staffing standard, four clinics count as large. A large clinic is one averaging over 80 in-person visits a day [2]. The clinic directory's Q3 2026 averages put these four above that line:

- **Harbor Point (HBP):** 118 visits a day [3]
- **Northgate (NGT):** 102 visits a day [3]
- **Riverside (RVS):** 94 visits a day [3]
- **Elm Park (ELP):** 85 visits a day [3]

The other five clinics are medium or small. Northbridge, Riverbend, and Elmhurst are at 52, 46, and 38, and Cedar Hollow is at 31 [3]. Medium is 40 to 80 visits and small is under 40 [2].

Large clinics need 3 physicians or NPs on site, 2 MAs per clinician, 2 RNs including a designated charge nurse, and 4 front desk staff [2].

Bands are reset every quarter from the directory's visit column, so this list can change. The September 2026 standard replaced the 2025 version, which set the large threshold at over 90 visits [1][2]. Under the old threshold, Elm Park would have been medium.

Right now, we charge nothing. The October 2026 revision eliminated the no-show fee: "Halcyon no longer charges patients for missed appointments" [1]. It took effect October 5, 2026 and replaces the 2025 policy in full [1].

- **Missed appointment with no cancellation:** no charge. It counts as a no-show only if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead [1].
- **Older fees:** any no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 that are still unpaid are waived. Revenue Cycle Management will reverse them on patient statements, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [1].
- **Former policy:** the 2025 policy charged a $25 fee for each no-show after the second in a 12-month period, and it did not bill Medicaid or sliding-fee patients [2]. That policy no longer applies.

The knowledge base doesn't give a response time for Tallgrass Survey, because Tallgrass isn't a live support vendor for Halcyon.

- **Tallgrass isn't in the vendor support matrix.** The matrix lists the vendors that support live Halcyon systems and their P1–P3 response times. Tallgrass doesn't appear there [3]. The matrix says vendors that don't yet support a live system aren't listed, and their support terms are agreed when the contract is signed [3].
- **Tallgrass is a proposed vendor, not yet contracted.** Its record shows a business associate agreement that is not executed, with the order form on hold until it is [1]. The planned service is post-visit patient satisfaction surveys by SMS and email [1].
- **No PHI may be shared yet.** Under the HIPAA privacy policy, no patient information can go to Tallgrass until the agreement is signed, including for test files or pilots [1].

If you need Tallgrass's support terms, they would need to be set in the contract, which is still pending. The IT Service Desk (extension 4357) is the route for any live-system problem [3].

Yes. Halcyon pairs every new clinical hire with a preceptor, and that pairing lasts 90 days [1].

- **Structure:** Weekly check-ins for the first month, then every other week after that. The preceptor signs off on the competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [1].
- **Early schedule:** Days 4–5 are shadowing at the home clinic with the preceptor [1].

Northwind's onboarding buddy is a separate arrangement. It's a named person who walks new hires through their first two weeks, and the Northwind guide doesn't give a set end date [2].

rows.answer:
Patient incidents at Halcyon are logged in **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy doesn't set a specific deadline for that filing. The steps around it do have timings.

**Where it goes:** SafeReport. Reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**Who files:** Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event [1]. The attending clinician also discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

**How soon:**
- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe, following the clinical escalation protocol and calling 911 if needed [1][4].
- **Immediately:** Tell the charge nurse on shift. If the clinic has no charge nurse on shift, tell the clinic manager [1]. The charge nurse coordinates the response.
- **Within 1 hour:** For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1].
- **Within 72 hours:** For Level 1 and Level 2 events, QPS charters the root cause analysis (RCA) team [1].
- **Within 45 calendar days:** The RCA must be completed from the date the event became known [1].

If you're unsure of the severity, report at the higher level. QPS will reclassify if needed [1]. Levels run from 1 (sentinel event) to 4 (near miss) [1].

**Privacy incidents are different.** A suspected privacy incident, such as a misdirected fax, a lost device, or a chart left open on an unattended screen, goes to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours, by email to privacy@halcyon.example or via the compliance hotline [5].

The `/incident declare` command you use at Northwind doesn't apply here. I found no Halcyon equivalent to it in the knowledge base.

rows.answer:
Yes, Northwind's approach is close to yours, though its documents say "blameless" rather than "just culture." Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution. It looks at the system and the process rather than individuals, and names appear only in the timeline [2][3]. Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [2][3].

The incident commander picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure [2]. The commander coordinates the response and does not debug, so the author is typically someone from the responding team. For example, the August 14 ingest outage (INC-2291) was a SEV-1 with Oluwaseun Adeyemi as incident commander, and its postmortem was written by Priya Raman with the ingest team [1][5].

I didn't find a documented rule on whether the author is also the one who decides the root cause, or on how the review is approved beyond the reliability meeting.

rows.answer:
Halcyon Health is the organization that runs the EHR (Meridian), so its policies are the relevant ones. I found no periodic need-based access recertification for Halcyon's EHR, and no rule for what happens if nobody signs off on access.

**What Halcyon does do**
- The compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection. Unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [1].
- Access to clinical systems is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1].
- Every break-the-glass event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. If the reason is unclear, the manager is asked to confirm it [2].

**What I couldn't find for Halcyon**
- A scheduled review in which managers confirm each user still needs their access.
- A rule that removes access when no one confirms it.

**Northwind Labs for comparison**
Northwind's information security policy does require quarterly access reviews run by each team lead. Access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [3]. Northwind doesn't operate the EHR, so this doesn't apply to Halcyon's logs, but it is the only recertification-with-automatic-revocation rule I found.

If you need Halcyon's recertification procedure, ask the Privacy Officer or the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui, per the systems inventory [5]), since it may exist outside the documents I searched.

rows.answer:
At Northwind, any tool that will process customer data has to go through the `#vendor-review` security review first [11]. I didn't find a typical turnaround time for that review in the knowledge base.

**Halcyon requirements for AI tools with patient data**

Halcyon's rules apply to Halcyon staff, not Northwind. Any tool that will handle PHI needs all of the following [1]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement (BAA) with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

Staff email the Privacy Officer and the HIPAA Security Officer to start this [1]. Only tools on the approved list may receive PHI, and any other AI tool is off-limits [1][6].

**How long it takes**

Halcyon's guidance says the typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [1].

**Currently approved tools**

- Quillon Ambient: PHI allowed, pilot clinics only (Riverside and Elm Park), with patient verbal consent at every visit [1]. Its BAA was executed July 30, 2026 [7].
- Meridian draft replies: PHI allowed, but a clinician must edit or approve every reply before it is sent [1].
- Halcyon Assist: PHI not allowed, policy questions only [1].

The Halcyon equivalent is the **system steward for Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), Felix Brandt**. The Halcyon app, which handles bill pay, is owned by DHE-PE [4]. Stewards approve changes to their team's systems [1].

Yes, for a purely cosmetic change, his approval is enough on its own. Halcyon classes cosmetic changes as minor, and minor changes need steward approval only [1]. Significant changes need three things: the steward's approval, clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao (or her delegate, Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at the weekly CSCAB [1].

The tweak stays minor only if it doesn't touch anything that makes a change significant. That includes patient-facing automation, the patient app's clinical content, medication information, orders or results routing, and CDS rules or alerts [1]. A bill-pay layout change is unlikely to hit those, but if the change adds any messages or touches clinical content, treat it as significant.

Note that the policy was revised in September 2026 after IR-0412 [1]. I didn't find anything in the knowledge base that suggests a separate rule for bill-pay screens.

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs (INC-2340, October double invoices):** The fix is idempotency on invoice creation. Each invoice creation now carries a key per workspace and billing period, so a re-run of the month-end job can't create a second invoice for the same period [8][10]. The root cause was a payment-provider webhook that timed out, after which retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [8]. Engineering also added a daily reconciliation report comparing invoices with charges, marked done [10]. The Slack record says the PR merged and deployed on October 6 [8], while the status sheet lists the fix as shipped October 8 [10]. An alert for provider webhook timeouts during billing batches is still open, due November 6 [10].

**Halcyon Health (IR-0412, September duplicate reminders):** The fix is also an idempotency key, this time on each reminder, built from patient, medication and scheduled time. A reminder whose key already exists is never sent again [1]. The incident happened because two job runners were active during a scheduler cutover, and neither checked whether a reminder had already gone out [1]. Halcyon added process controls too: scheduler cutovers need a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off [1], and the runbook must state how double-running is prevented [2]. Reminder wording was also changed to tell patients they don't need to retake a dose they already took [1].

**Northwind Labs has a holiday change freeze. Halcyon Health has no IT freeze.**

**Northwind Labs:** The holiday freeze runs from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027. Only standard and emergency changes ship in that window [1]. Rollbacks are allowed at any time, freeze or not [1][4]. The on-call notes also say the week of December 22 falls inside the freeze, so expect a quiet week but stay reachable [2]. The rota for shifts starting December 29 onward is due by December 15 [2].

Northwind also has a month-end billing freeze. No normal changes to Ledger are allowed from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually the 2nd [1][3]. For this month, that freeze started Friday, October 30 and runs until invoices are sent, expected November 2 [3]. Between now and the holidays, the next month-end window is the last business day of November, so check the dates before planning Ledger work.

**Halcyon Health:** The October Juniper steering committee notes state "No IT freeze at Halcyon" [7]. They do add that clinic managers asked that pilot training not land in the week of December 21 [7]. Halcyon's staff-leave rules also treat December 20 to January 2 as a special approval period, but that concerns leave, not change control [5].

Both clients still follow their normal change approval processes during the open periods. Northwind normal changes need sign-off from the owning team's change approver [1]. Halcyon changes to clinical systems go through CSCAB, and the dates for cutover and go-live are set by CSCAB, not the project register [6].

**Err higher in both cases.** Northwind's rule is "when unsure, declare higher; downgrading is cheap" [3]. Halcyon's policy says "When unsure, report at the higher level" [2].

**Northwind Labs (incidents)**
- Whoever declares the incident picks the initial severity. The incident commander (IC) can raise or lower it at any time [3].
- SEV-1 is data loss or a full ingest or pipeline outage for a cell. SEV-2 is a partial outage or degradation affecting many customers. SEV-3 is a single-customer or non-critical issue [1].

**Halcyon Health (patient safety events)**
- The event is reported at the higher level of the four (sentinel, adverse event with harm, no-harm event, near miss). The Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) team will reclassify it if needed [2].
- The policy does not say who else can change a rating. Your first step is still to make the patient safe and tell the charge nurse, or the clinic manager if no charge nurse is on shift [2].

**Northwind's helpdesk vendor (Hollowpine Software Co.)** is waiting on a DPA negotiation. Hollowpine's DPA draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines have been with legal since August. The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [8]. Interim cover is security exception SEC-EX-117, approved by the Head of Security on August 24, 2026 [8]. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [8].

**Halcyon's patient survey vendor (Tallgrass Survey Co.)** is waiting on a business associate agreement (BAA). The draft arrived in August 2026, and the security risk assessment passed with conditions in September [6]. The open issue is data retention: Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable survey responses for 5 years for benchmarking, while Halcyon will accept 18 months [6]. Halcyon's Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [6]. The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [6]. No PHI may be shared with Tallgrass before then [6].

Until these are resolved, Halcyon collects post-visit satisfaction scores with the in-app survey [6][11].

**Halcyon offers the bigger discount: 20% versus Northwind's 15%.** The comparison has caveats, though.

- **Northwind:** Annual prepayment on the Growth plan earns a 15% discount, equivalent to $12,240 per year [1]. A September 2026 sales memo confirms the 15% prepayment discount is unchanged [4].
- **Halcyon:** Self-pay patients who pay in full on the day of service get a 20% prompt-pay discount [3]. This applies to visit fees such as the $165 new-patient visit [3].
- **Halcyon exception:** The 20% prompt-pay discount does not apply to vaccine and injectable prices, which are already set at cost plus administration [2].

The two offers are not like-for-like. Northwind's discount is on an annual software subscription, while Halcyon's is on a single self-pay visit or service paid in full that day.

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs:** The incident commander (IC) can approve an emergency change, but only during a declared incident. The IC is the person paged when someone runs `/incident declare` [3][4]. The change must then be reviewed retroactively by the owning team's change approver within two business days [3]. Approvers are named per team, for example Priya Raman for Data Plane and Tomasz Wierzbicki for Security [2].

**Halcyon Health:** The on-call medical director may approve an emergency change to a clinical system [5]. Emergency changes are made to stop ongoing patient harm [1]. The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews the change at its next meeting [1]. CSCAB meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1]. The on-call medical director is reached through the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [5].

The two organizations differ in who approves and what triggers it. Northwind relies on a declared incident, and the review is done by the owning team's approver within two business days. Halcyon relies on the on-call medical director, and the review is done by a committee at its next meeting. The Halcyon review timing is not stated more precisely in the sources I found.
